prompt.context: Your client is a mobile service provider in an Asian country. They were targeting the high and medium segments in the country. Recently they acquired another service provider which targeted the lower segment of the market. The two companies had two different brands before the merger, and they kept both brands after the merge.
prompt.question: To the CEO's surprise, the overall pre-tax profit has been lower than the combined pre-tax profit of the two companies when they were not merged. You are hired to figure out why and how the company can improve that.

framework: Use the profitability formula: Profit = (Price - Variable Cost) x Volume - Fixed Cost
Consider product mix across the two brands (H brand targeting high/medium segments; L brand targeting lower segment)
Since costs have been optimized post-merger, focus on revenue drivers: price, volume, and mix
Decompose revenue by brand, then further decompose L brand by sub-segment (LM = middle income, LL = low income)
Investigate whether a mix shift within L brand toward lower-revenue sub-segments explains the profit decline
Explore root causes of any mix shift: demand changes, competitor actions, product cannibalization, or 4P changes (promotion in particular)
Validate competitor-driven churn hypothesis through customer database analysis and targeted surveys

questions.prompt: Has pricing changed for either the H brand or the L brand after the merger?
questions.guidance: Pricing plans for both brands are unchanged. However, actual revenue per customer per month is flat for H brand and decreasing for L brand. The candidate should recognize this discrepancy and focus attention on the L brand.

questions.prompt: Within the L brand, what sub-segments exist, and has the customer mix shifted?
questions.guidance: L brand serves two sub-segments: LM (middle income) and LL (low income). The mix has been shifting toward LL customers. Since LL customers generate lower revenue per user than LM customers, even with flat total volume the average revenue per L brand customer falls, reducing overall profit.
Volume has not changed. The profit decline is entirely explained by the mix shift within L brand toward the lower-revenue LL sub-segment, not by volume loss.

questions.prompt: What could be causing the mix shift toward the LL sub-segment within L brand?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates consider: (1) demand shift — customer preferences moving toward lower plans; (2) competitor actions — a competitor may have poached LM customers; (3) product cannibalization — within L brand between LM and LL; (4) 4P changes — the company promoted heavily on the LL plan, attracting more LL customers. Candidate should rule out cannibalization (between sub-segments and between H and L brands — both confirmed absent) and identify that heavy promotion of the LL plan drew net-new LL customers while existing LM customers may have been lost to a competitor.

questions.prompt: How would you verify whether a competitor is taking LM customers?
questions.guidance: Review the historical customer database to identify LM customer churn patterns. Conduct a targeted survey of churned LM customers asking: (1) Why did they leave? (2) Which provider did they choose and why? This validates the competitor-poaching hypothesis with primary data before drawing conclusions.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the possible reasons for the mix shift within L brand toward the lower-revenue LL sub-segment?

categories.name: Demand / Customer behavior
ideas: Natural income-level shift in addressable market
Customers downgrading plans due to economic conditions

categories.name: Competitor actions
ideas: A competitor launched an attractive offer targeting LM customers
Competitor pricing undercut the LM plan, pulling LM customers away

categories.name: Product cannibalization
ideas: LL plan features overlap with LM plan, causing LM customers to trade down
Lack of differentiation between the two sub-segment plans

categories.name: 4P / Marketing
ideas: Heavy promotion of LL plan attracted net-new LL customers, growing LL share
Insufficient marketing investment in LM plan relative to LL plan
Sales force incentivized to sign up LL customers

recommendation: The profit decline is driven by a mix shift within the L brand toward lower-revenue LL sub-segment customers, not by price changes or volume decline
Primary driver is likely a combination of heavy LL promotion (growing LL share) and possible competitor poaching of higher-value LM customers
risks: If the competitor has a sustained pricing or product advantage for the LM segment, recovery of LM customers may require price concessions that compress margin
Over-investing in LL promotion further deteriorates revenue mix
next_steps: Analyze historical customer database to quantify LM churn rate and timing relative to competitor activity
Survey churned LM customers to confirm whether a competitor offer triggered switching
Reassess promotion strategy: reduce LL promotion or add LM-targeted retention campaigns
Consider product differentiation between LM and LL plans to reduce the appeal of downgrading
